newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Volvo in spotlight after Electrolux plan.
newsitem.headline: Volvo in spotlight after Electrolux plan.

text.p: Pressure has increased on AB Volvo's new chief executive to prove he was the right choice for the Swedish vehicle maker following Electrolux's huge restructuring programme, analysts said on Friday.
Leif Johansson left AB Electrolux this spring after three years as its chief executive and having spent most of his working life with the consumer appliances company.

After just two months at the helm of Electrolux, Johansson's successor, Michael Treschow, announced on Thursday he would close plants and lay off 12,000 staff in a 2.5 billion crown ($321.3 million) restructuring programme.
Electrolux shares rallied 64 crowns to 529 after the news and extended gains on Friday, rocketing another 63 to 592.
"It's clear people would prefer to have Treschow in charge instead of Johansson," one analyst said.
"It will be important how the large domestic investors interpret his presentation. But I think they will give him a few months before they deliver the verdict," an analyst said.
Analysts are looking forward to Johansson showing his colours at Volvo, and some say they will be expecting some sort of move in the next few months.
Most agree his comments at a Volvo seminar at the company's home base in Swedish west coast city in Gothenburg this week were colourless.
Johansson told the seminar on Thursday the company was considering several business deals, including acquisitions, and pledged to continue trimming costs.
"At the (Volvo seminar) he didn't announce anything revolutionary," Dresdner Kleinwort Benson analyst Karl-Johan Bonnevier told Reuters.
"I think he will probably be announcing something by the second quarter or soon after that when he has gone through the strategy."
Treschow, who has a reputation as a cost cutter with a focus on shareholder value, may have had an easier time putting changes through at Electrolux as a newcomer than Johansson had.
"Johansson may have a few ideas for Volvo which he didn't manage to do at Electrolux. It's easier when you come to a new place and have a clean table to work with," said Bonnevier.
Most analysts agreed, however, that Volvo has already undergone radical changes and clearly less needs to be done.

"The market will probably need to see decisive action from Johansson in the second quarter or so in order for him to convince investors that he won't be the same vague character he was at Electrolux," said an analyst, who asked to be unnamed.
Others said the criticism of Johansson was unjustified and much of the cost-savings plan was likely the work of Johansson over the previous 12 months.
"The market is giving Treschow a god-like status," UBS analyst Andrew Griffin said. "Trying to cut 11 percent of the workforce will be a great challenge to the company. It's a costly programme."
Paribas engineering analyst Christian Diebitsch said weak markets haunted Johansson's tenure at Electrolux but that he had done a lot for the company.

"Since 1989 they cut the workforce by 27 percent and operating costs by seven percent, while over that period compound average sales growth was three percent, so it's not that he's been sitting still," he added.
Another analyst pointed out it was not a question of taking a bad manager out of Electrolux and dumping him on Volvo.
"I think his talents are better used in the car industry, but having said that, I think he has an awful lot to prove," the analyst said.
-- Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1003 ($ = 7.781 Swedish Crowns)
